recipe.history:
Cranberry sauce as a prepared condiment has roots in Indigenous North American cooking that predate European contact by centuries. The Algonquin, Ojibwe, and other northeastern woodland peoples used wild cranberries — known by various names including "ibimi" in the Wampanoag language and "atoqua" in Algonquin — both as food and as a dye, mixing the berries with dried meat and animal fat to make pemmican, the high-calorie travel food that sustained people through long winters. European colonists in New England encountered cranberries in the early seventeenth century and began cooking them into sauces and preserves, sweetened with honey or maple syrup and later with refined sugar as trade routes expanded. The commercial cranberry industry took hold in Massachusetts and New Jersey in the early nineteenth century, and by the mid-1800s canned cranberry sauce had become a widely distributed commodity. Ocean Spray Cranberries, founded as a cooperative in 1930, nationalized the cranberry's presence in the American pantry and made cranberry sauce a fixture of the Thanksgiving and Christmas table — a role it has occupied ever since with remarkable durability. Brie cheese, meanwhile, is one of France's oldest and most celebrated soft-ripened cheeses, produced in the region east of Paris that bears its name since at least the eighth century, when Charlemagne reportedly declared it among the finest foods in France after tasting it at a monastery near Meaux.

The Christmas burger as a category belongs to the broader American tradition of seasonal menu items — the limited-time holiday offering that signals festivity and indulgence. The combination of cranberry sauce, brie, and spiced walnuts represents a direct translation of the classic holiday cheese board into burger form. This translation is not merely clever; it is culinarily sound. Cranberry's bright acidity cuts through brie's rich, mushroomy funk in exactly the same way it cuts through turkey fat at Thanksgiving — both are high-fat proteins whose richness benefits from the berry's tartness. Rosemary brioche buns evoke the pine and evergreen aromatics of the winter holiday season and bring a herbal note that ties the sweet-savory components together. The spiced walnut adds crunch, bitterness, warmth, and the faint autumnal sweetness of cinnamon and brown sugar — the flavors of a holiday kitchen rendered crispy and compact.

My most vivid Christmas cooking memory involves a kitchen that was too small for the number of people trying to use it simultaneously. My grandmother's house in Vermont, on a December twenty-fourth when all the cousins had arrived and the kitchen smelled like pine resin from the boughs on the mantle and mulled wine from the pot simmering on the back burner. Somebody had made a brie en croûte that burst in the oven and sent a river of warm, runny cheese across the baking sheet, and instead of being upset, my grandmother simply declared that we would eat it with cranberry sauce from a spoon. We stood around the kitchen counter eating warm brie and cranberry sauce with crackers and bread scraps for twenty minutes, and it was better than anything that appeared at the formal dinner table that followed. That memory — that combination of melted brie, tart cranberry, and the warmth of a crowded winter kitchen — is what this burger is trying to reconstitute in a form you can hold in both hands.

The medium-rare philosophy is especially important on a holiday burger, because the inclination toward festivity can lead cooks to overcomplicate and to overcook. The centerpiece of this burger is the patty. The cranberry, the brie, the spiced walnuts — these are ornaments. Beautiful ones, meaningful ones, but ornaments. At 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C), the beef remains the centerpiece it should be: juicy, rich, and deeply flavored, a canvas for the holiday accompaniments rather than a structural filler. Cook it to well done and the patty recedes from the flavor composition entirely, becoming merely a vehicle for the toppings. The burger is not a cheese board with meat hidden inside it. It is a beef burger dressed for a party, and the beef must be dressed to its best advantage — which is always, and without exception, medium rare.
ingredients: 2 tsp fresh rosemary, very finely minced
2 large eggs (1 for dough, 1 beaten for egg wash)
8 oz ripe Brie de Meaux or double-cream brie, rind left on, thinly sliced
1 tsp fresh rosemary, very finely minced
instructions: 1. Make the rosemary brioche buns: Bloom the yeast with warm water and 1 tablespoon of sugar for 5 minutes. Add flour, remaining sugar, salt, minced rosemary, 1 egg, warm milk, and softened butter. Knead in a stand mixer with the dough hook 8 to 10 minutes until smooth, slightly tacky, and elastic. Rise in an oiled bowl for 1 to 1 1/2 hours until doubled. Shape into 4 tight rounds, proof on a parchment-lined baking sheet for 45 minutes. Brush with beaten egg. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15 to 18 minutes until deep golden brown and fragrant with rosemary. Cool completely on a rack.

2. Make the cranberry sauce: Combine the cranberries, sugar, orange juice, water, orange zest, cinnamon, cloves, and salt in a medium saucepan. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat, stirring to dissolve the sugar. Reduce to a steady simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, 10 to 12 minutes until the cranberries have burst and the sauce has thickened to a jammy consistency. Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate. The sauce will thicken further as it cools.

3. Make the spiced candied walnuts: Melt the butter in a skillet over medium heat. Add the walnuts and stir to coat. Add the brown sugar, cinnamon, cayenne, and salt, stirring constantly for 3 to 4 minutes until the sugar has melted and caramelized around the walnuts and they are fragrant and deeply toasted. Spread on a parchment-lined plate to cool. They will harden as they cool. Roughly chop before assembly.
4. Make the herbed mayonnaise: Stir together the mayonnaise, minced rosemary, Dijon mustard, grated garlic, and salt in a small bowl until combined. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Form the burger patties: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (8 oz / 227g each). Gently shape into patties approximately 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple into the center. Combine the salt, pepper, and dried thyme and season both sides of each patty generously just before cooking.

6. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook the patties 3 to 4 minutes on the first side without pressing, building a deep crust. Flip once. Immediately arrange the brie slices generously over each patty, overlapping to cover the surface. Cover the pan and cook 2 to 3 more minutes until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) and the brie is melted and beginning to pool at the edges. Transfer to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
7. Split the rosemary brioche buns and toast cut-side down in the hot skillet for 60 to 90 seconds until lightly golden.

8. Assemble: Spread the herbed mayonnaise on both bun halves. On the bottom bun, place a leaf of butter lettuce or frisée. Spoon a generous layer of cranberry sauce directly onto the lettuce. Place the brie-topped patty over the cranberry sauce. Scatter the chopped spiced candied walnuts over the melted brie. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Cap with the top bun. Serve immediately — this is a Christmas miracle in hand-held form.
